analysis.one_liner: Repeals billions of dollars in tax breaks, royalties relief, and federal financing for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of the ten committees it was sent to, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a long list of special tax breaks and federal support for fossil fuel companies: it repeals deductions and credits for oil, gas, and coal producers, raises the royalty rate companies pay for drilling and mining on federal land from 12.5% to 18.75%, ends royalty relief for offshore drilling, removes liability caps for offshore spills, and bars federal agencies and export banks from financing fossil fuel projects [S2][S3]. It would also make the coal excise tax that funds black lung benefits for miners permanent [S3]. It was referred to ten House committees, none of which ever acted on it [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers benefit because companies would lose deductions and credits they now use to reduce their taxes, and the government would collect higher royalties on oil, gas, and coal taken from federal land [S2][S3]. Coal miners with black lung disease benefit from a permanently higher excise tax on coal that funds their benefits [S3]. Communities near pipelines carrying tar sands oil benefit from the removal of liability limits that currently cap what a spilling company must pay [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, coal miners, Gulf coast communities

how_it_helps.text: Terminates a series of tax provisions that benefit fossil fuel producers, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion for oil and gas wells, and capital gains treatment for coal royalties [S2][S3].
Raises the minimum royalty rate on federal coal, oil, and gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75%, so the public gets more for resources taken from federal land [S3].
Repeals royalty relief provisions that reduce what offshore and deep-well drillers owe the government, and raises the excise tax that funds the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund [S2][S3].
Removes the liability cap on offshore facilities and onshore pipelines carrying tar sands oil, so companies responsible for spills would pay their full damages instead of a capped amount [S3].

Blocks fossil fuel companies from receiving pandemic-era federal loans and loan guarantees under the CARES Act, and bars the Export-Import Bank and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation from financing fossil fuel projects [S2][S3].

Makes the coal excise tax rates that fund the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund permanent at higher rates ($1.38 per ton for underground coal), securing benefits for miners with black lung disease [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, natural gas, and coal companies would pay more in taxes and royalties and could no longer shift some costs onto the public through liability caps and royalty relief [S2][S3]. Large banks and financial institutions with over $10 billion in assets would lose their exemption from cleanup liability under the superfund law for polluted fossil fuel sites they finance [S3]. Some of these costs could be passed through to consumers in the form of higher fuel prices [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies; large banks

drawbacks.text: Raising royalties, ending deductions, and imposing a new 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico production would increase costs for producers, some of which could reach consumers through higher fuel prices [S3].

The bill terminates the Department of Energy's Fossil Energy Research and Development Program and the carbon oxide sequestration (45Q) credit, eliminating federal support for research on and deployment of carbon capture technology that many climate experts consider necessary [S3].

Restrictions on financing fossil fuel projects, including a ban on new bank stakes in fossil fuel businesses and a moratorium on new federal oil, gas, and coal leases during the COVID emergency, could raise financing costs for energy projects and affect jobs in oil, gas, and coal regions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would transfer tens of billions in tax breaks and below-market royalties from fossil fuel producers back to taxpayers, put full cleanup liability on the companies that cause spills, and secure funding for black lung benefits. The main honest objections are that some costs would flow to consumers as higher energy prices, that the outright termination of carbon capture incentives and fossil energy R&D removes tools some climate policy experts want to keep, and that communities dependent on fossil fuel production would bear adjustment costs. On balance the bill is a straightforward reversal of long-standing industry preferences at industry expense.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to ten House committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them ever held a hearing, marked it up, or brought it to the floor, so it died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2020 on July 24, 2020, with 15 Democratic cosponsors [S4][S5].

The same day, the House referred it to ten committees, including Ways and Means, Natural Resources, and Energy and Commerce — a referral pattern that requires every committee with jurisdiction to act before the bill can advance [S5].
Over the following six weeks, small subcommittees in four of those committees received pieces of the bill, but no full committee ever took action on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired on January 3, 2021, when the 116th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers kept every tax break, royalty rate, liability cap, and federal financing channel the bill would have ended, and the large financial institutions that would have become liable for polluted sites kept their exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies and their lenders

against.what_they_did: None of the ten committees to which the bill was referred ever reported it, held a hearing, or allowed a vote during the remaining five and a half months of the Congress [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All 16 supporters in the House — the sponsor and 15 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill; because no vote ever occurred, the partisan shape of opposition was never tested on the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill strips away their deductions (intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, LIFO accounting), credits, royalty relief on federal leases, and CARES Act loan eligibility, and raises their federal royalty rate to 18.75%. The industry's gain under the status quo comes from tax provisions and below-market public resources — the public's cost [S2][S3].

The bill repeals percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal royalties, ends the refined coal production credit, raises the black lung excise tax, and requires an 18.75% federal royalty. Coal extraction on public land has long been leased at rates that return little to the Treasury [S3].

The bill removes the superfund-law exemption that shields banks with $10 billion or more in assets from cleanup liability at sites they finance, and bars banks receiving pandemic-era federal backstops from taking ownership stakes in fossil fuel businesses. The exemption currently shifts cleanup costs of failed sites onto taxpayers [S3].

industries.industry: Offshore and pipeline operators (including tar sands transporters)
industries.note: The bill removes statutory liability caps, so a company that spills would pay its full damages rather than a capped amount, and would lose the tax deduction for spill cleanup costs. Caps currently put the excess cost of major spills on the public [S3].
The bill repeals the corporate income tax exemption for master limited partnerships whose income comes from fossil fuel activities, ending a tax advantage over other businesses [S3].
